content: 1. Conduct comprehensive assessments to identify sources of information that can be utilized for analyzing questions, concerns, information gaps, and circulating narratives, including misinformation and disinformation, across all relevant sectors. Use these findings to determine the necessary risk communication and community engagement response measures. 2. Establish structures to support a unified One Voice approach, ensuring that trained and designated spokespersons from various sectors deliver consistent and accurate communications. 3. Ensure that all stakeholders' digital channels provide basic, credible, and accurate influenza information that is easily accessible, shareable, optimized for search engines, and tailored to relevant audiences. 4. Initiate response activities in alignment with the risk communication and community engagement plan as soon as possible, even if the facts are not yet fully clear or complete. Use language that acknowledges uncertainty, such as: The situation is uncertain, and we share your concerns. We are seeking answers and will keep you updated as new information becomes available. 5. Involve all stakeholders and partners in response activities. Collaborate with affected communities and stakeholders to co-create and disseminate influenza prevention messages, materials, and health guidance, translating the latest scientific findings into actionable advice. 6. Key messages should focus on raising awareness about how to stay safe and whom to contact regarding concerns about animals or humans. Use images and videos to explain complex concepts effectively. 7. Implement social-behavioral feedback mechanisms and issue social listening and infodemic insights reports. Use these findings to enhance the accuracy, quality, and accessibility of health information. 8. Minimize public exposure to potentially infected animals and other sources of contamination. Individuals exposed to such animals should practice proper personal hygiene, including frequent handwashing, and seek medical attention promptly if illness develops. 9. Collaborate with the animal health sector and other relevant entities to reduce the risk of transmission of animal influenza viruses to humans in ways that are acceptable to the public, producers, and traders. 10. Identify at-risk groups when influenza viruses are circulating in animal populations. These groups include individuals who handle live poultry, slaughter or process poultry, work in the poultry industry, or engage in outdoor activities involving wild birds or swine. 11. The general public should minimize contact with animals in areas affected by animal influenza viruses, such as farms or live animal markets. Children, older adults, pregnant women, and immunocompromised individuals should avoid handling animals or their by-products. 12. Practice good hygiene by washing hands frequently with soap and water or using alcohol-based hand rubs, especially after contact with animals or their environments. 13. Use appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) when handling animals or their waste in areas where influenza viruses may be present. PPE should include waterproof protective clothing, particulate respirators, gloves, and boots. Proper training on the use and disposal of PPE is essential. 14. Monitor individuals involved in high-risk tasks, such as culling infected birds or cleaning contaminated premises, for at least seven days after exposure. Any symptomatic individuals should be considered suspect cases and managed accordingly. 15. Conduct risk assessments to evaluate the degree of exposure and update these assessments periodically. Consider post-exposure antiviral prophylaxis on a case-by-case basis for high-risk individuals. 16. Promote thorough cooking of poultry and poultry products. Educate the public on safe food preparation and consumption practices to prevent cross-contamination. 17. Ensure that traditional food market hygiene and biosecurity measures are assessed and improved where possible. Encourage good animal production practices to reduce the risk of influenza virus emergence and spread. 18. Eggs, poultry meat, and other poultry products can be safely consumed if properly cooked and handled during food preparation. Separate raw meat from cooked or ready-to-eat foods to avoid cross-contamination. 19. Wash hands, surfaces, and utensils thoroughly with soap and water before and after handling raw poultry or eggs. Cooked meat should not be placed back onto surfaces that previously held raw meat. 20. Report sick or unexpectedly dead animals to veterinary authorities immediately and comply with official measures, such as animal movement restrictions. Avoid slaughtering or consuming animals showing signs of disease or that have died unexpectedly. 21. Individuals exposed to potentially infected animals should seek medical care promptly if they feel unwell and inform their healthcare provider about their possible exposure. 22. Consider immunizing individuals at high risk of exposure to avian influenza viruses with the seasonal influenza vaccine to protect against seasonal influenza and facilitate the detection of avian influenza infections. However, this will not reduce the risk of avian influenza infection itself.
